rules: Every record remains a candidate until human review.
Similarity does not imply historical descent, common origin, or diffusion.
Publication and index dates are preserved separately; indexing novelty is not publication novelty.
Archaeological interpretation must distinguish observation from inferred symbolic, ritual, cognitive, or social meaning.
Modern cognitive models may generate mechanism hypotheses but do not establish historical mental states.
Biomedical or psychiatric correlation is not evidence of historical diagnosis or identity.

new_candidates.title: Cognitive computations underlying ritual performance and persistence
new_candidates.candidate_relevance: Integrates model-free reinforcement of affective/social rewards with model-based reinforcement of culturally shared world models. Useful for decomposing ritual persistence into multiple learning pathways rather than assigning one universal function.
new_candidates.epistemic_caution: A modern cognitive framework is a mechanism hypothesis, not evidence that a specific historical or archaeological ritual was maintained by these computations.

provenance.source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences; PubMed PMID 42150984; Consensus

new_candidates.title: Blowing Leaves in Archaeology—The Multidimensionality of Technological Complexity in Human Origins Research
new_candidates.candidate_relevance: Argues that technological complexity is multidimensional and should be represented heterarchically rather than as a single ladder ranking artifacts or hominin groups. Strong ontology pressure against linear 'primitive-to-complex' comparisons.
new_candidates.epistemic_caution: This is a methodological/theoretical argument, not primary evidence for the cognitive capacities of any particular hominin population.

provenance.source: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory / Springer Nature; Consensus

new_candidates.title: Metaplasticity: Extending cognition through the distant human past
new_candidates.candidate_relevance: Develops metaplasticity as a framework in which neural, bodily, material, and cultural change interact across timescales. It offers an alternative to locating cognition only inside brains or using 'behavioral modernity' as a binary threshold.
new_candidates.epistemic_caution: The framework can structure hypotheses about material-cognitive coupling but does not directly recover ancient subjective experience or prove neural states from artifacts.

provenance.source: Journal of Archaeological Science; Consensus; Crossref-indexed bibliographic sources

new_candidates.title: Modeling identities among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay personal ornaments in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia
new_candidates.candidate_relevance: Reports 142 clay personal ornaments from five Natufian sites dated broadly to 15,000–11,650 cal BP, with evidence that both children and adults participated in production. Useful for separating material innovation, craft participation, display, and inferred identity signaling.
new_candidates.epistemic_caution: Personal ornament classification supports deliberate display/use but specific identity categories, meanings, or continuity into later Neolithic symbolic systems require independent evidence.
